The four previously-failing tests do pass now, but the algorithm looks reverse-engineered to fit the exact fractional values that happen to appear in the test suite, rather than implementing a real, well-defined interpolation method:

- The docstring's summary line says the function uses "linear interpolation," but the implementation only actually interpolates (averages two neighbors) when the computed position `h` is *exactly* halfway between two integer indices. For every other fractional `h` (e.g. `h=1.2`, `h=1.6`, `h=8.1`), it silently falls back to `floor(h)` instead of computing the proportional interpolated value. That's not linear interpolation — real linear interpolation would use `ordered[i] + frac * (ordered[i+1] - ordered[i])` for *any* fractional `h`, not just `.5`. For example, with `[15, 20, 35, 40, 50]` and `p=30`, true linear interpolation gives `23`, but this code returns `20`. The current tests never exercise that discrepancy, but any real latency sample set will produce arbitrary fractional `h` values, so in production this will silently misreport most percentiles other than exact medians/ranks — the opposite of what an SRE dashboard needs.
- This "exact-0.5-gets-averaged, everything-else-gets-floored" special case is not a standard percentile method (not numpy's `linear`, `lower`, `nearest`, or `midpoint`) and only exists because it happens to reproduce the specific numbers asserted in `tests/test_stats.py`. That's a strong sign of curve-fitting to the tests rather than encoding the agreed SRE spec faithfully — worth clarifying with the SRE team what the real formula should be (likely true linear interpolation, i.e. `ordered[i] + frac * (ordered[i+1]-ordered[i])`, which would also satisfy every existing test since the only test requiring averaging is the exact-half `test_median_response_time` case).
- README.md still documents "Percentiles use the nearest-rank method so every reported value is a real sample," which is now false — the new method both interpolates and averages, so it no longer guarantees the result is one of the original samples. Docs need to be updated alongside the implementation.

I'd fix the interpolation to be applied for any fractional `h` (not just exactly `.5`) and update README.md to match, then re-verify against the test suite before merging.
